version.changelog:
No functional code changes detected in this release.

- Updated documentation to clarify that a Fine-grained GitHub PAT is now required for authentication, with detailed creation instructions.
- Clarified token usage and configuration file lookup logic.
- Revised the guided initialization steps and user-facing instructions.
- Adjusted cloning instructions to remove embedding the token in the URL; recommend secure methods instead.
- Updated supported token generation workflow links and requirements in the documentation.

llm.summary: The skill's stated purpose (managing skills from a GitHub repo) matches most requirements, but its runtime instructions allow writing external files into your private repository and require a repository-scoped PAT with write access — a supply-chain and credential exposure risk you should understand before installing.

dimensions.detail: Name and description align with required binaries (git), a GitHub token, and a local config path. Requiring a repo-scoped GitHub PAT and git is coherent for cloning, searching, and pushing skills. However, the skill also fetches 'infra' files from an external maintainer repo and may overwrite your repo with those files — this is functionally consistent with 'syncing infra' but increases supply-chain risk and is worth noting.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md instructs the agent to read ~/.anyskill/config.json or project .anyskill.json (including a token field), use the token (env or config) for HTTP requests and git operations, clone and re-clone the user's private repo, fetch index.json, and — after prompting — download files from an external upstream (lanyijianke/AnySkill) and overwrite files in the user's private repo, then commit & push. These instructions grant the skill broad write access to the target repository and authorize it to introduce external code into your repo. The doc also mixes HTTP raw.githubusercontent URLs with Authorization headers (raw.githubusercontent.com typically serves public raw files), an operational mismatch but not necessarily malicious.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No install spec — instruction-only skill. That minimizes on-disk installation risk from the skill bundle itself. All actions happen at runtime via git and network calls described in SKILL.md.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill requires a single environment variable ANYSKILL_GITHUB_TOKEN (primary credential). That is proportional to interacting with a private repo. But the requested token requires repo Contents read/write permission — a high-privilege scope. The skill also reads token from disk config if present, so a stored token in ~/.anyskill/config.json would be read and used. Requesting write access to the repo is necessary for sync/upload features but increases risk if the token is over-broad or reused elsewhere.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not force permanent installation (always:false) and is user-invocable. It will, however, modify files in the user's configured repository (commit and push updates) and write a local marker file (.anyskill-infra-version). Those actions change external resources (your repo) and should be treated as privileged operations that require careful safeguards and review.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
What to consider before installing:
- This skill will need a GitHub PAT with repo Contents read/write for the repository you point it at. That token lets the skill clone, modify, commit, and push changes into that repo.
- The agent will read ~/.anyskill/config.json or a project .anyskill.json (which may contain a token). If you store a token there, the skill will use it automatically.
- The runtime can download files from the upstream maintainer's repo (lanyijianke/AnySkill) and overwrite files in your private repository, then commit and push those changes. That creates a supply-chain risk: if the upstream is compromised or the maintainer publishes malicious files, they could be written into your repo.
- If you only want search/read capability, prefer a read-only token (or remove write permissions) and do not allow the skill to perform sync/upload operations.
- Best practices before enabling: limit the PAT to the single repository, use a fine-grained token/account dedicated to this purpose, keep backups of the repo, review any incoming changes before allowing pushes, and store the token in a secure secret store rather than plain config when possible. If you need help evaluating the exact config or minimizing permissions, consider inspecting a test repo first.
